Federer's vanquished opponent in the final, Soderling also praised his conquerer: "For me he is the best ever and I should know as I've player him many times," the world-ranked number 12 told CNN. LONDON, England (CNN) — Former world number one Pete Sampras has described newly crowned French Open champion Roger Federer as the greatest player in tennis history.

Federer’s victory equaled Sampras’s record of 14 men’s Grand Slam singles titles. The 37-year-old American, nicknamed “Pistol Pete” for his bullet-like serves, won a record 14 Grand Slam men’s singles titles during a 15-year career, although he never captured the trophy at Roland Garros.

By defeating Sweden’s Robin Soderling 6-1, 7-6, 6-4 in Sunday’s final, Federer claimed the French Open title, matched Sampras’s record and became only the sixth man in history to win all four majors.

**Debate: Is Federer the greatest player ever?**

According to Sampras, the achievement establishes the 27-year-old Swiss as the finest player ever to grace the game.

“What he’s done over the past five years has never, ever been done—and probably will never, ever happen again.

“Regardless of whether he won there or not, he goes down as the greatest ever. This just confirms it,” Sampras told *The Guardian* newspaper.

“I’m obviously happy for Roger. If there’s anyone who deserves it, it’s Roger. He’s come so close previously,” Sampras said of the new champion and world number two, who lost the previous three consecutive French Open finals to Spain’s Rafael Nadal.

Speaking exclusively to CNN after his victory, Federer said he was relieved to have bounced back after relinquishing the world number one ranking, as well as the Australian Open and Wimbledon titles, to Nadal in 2008.

“It’s been a fantastic day—to finally win the elusive French title was unbelievable. I always believed I was good enough to get it, but holding the trophy after all I’ve been through was just unbelievable. I’m so proud right now, you can’t believe it.

“For me, there was never a question of whether I was going to retire. I worked extremely hard in the off-season. All of a sudden, losing semifinals and finals wasn’t good enough for people anymore. But this victory is timely because I’ve proved many people wrong.”

The historic significance of the victory was not lost on Federer.

“The records mean a lot to me, especially after the last few years, when I realized that I was up there with the greatest players of all time. Of course, I like to break records because I look up to people like Sampras, Agassi, Connors and McEnroe. It’s so great to be up there with those players.”

However, in an ominous warning to his rivals, the champion said he was already looking toward his next conquest.

“I still feel like I have much more left in me. I’m only 27 years old, and I’d like to play for many more years to come. I hope I win many more titles.”

Federer’s defeated opponent in the final, Soderling, also praised his conqueror.

“For me, he is the best ever, and I should know, as I’ve played him many times,” the world number 12 told CNN.

Next for Federer is the third Grand Slam tournament of 2009, Wimbledon, where he will seek to go one better than Bjorn Borg by winning the event for a sixth time when it begins on June 22.

Federer’s historic weekend victory was also recognized by International Olympic Committee President Jacques Rogge, who likewise described the Swiss player as the best tennis has ever seen.

“Today, I wrote to Roger Federer to congratulate him on this unique success because I consider him to be the best player of all time,” Rogge told a media briefing in Brussels on Monday.

The IOC president revealed that, in the letter, he had expressed the hope that Federer would compete in the 2012 Olympic Games in London.

Federer added an Olympic gold medal to his collection of tennis accolades by winning the men’s doubles title with compatriot Stanislas Wawrinka in Beijing last year.

# Federer’s French Open triumph strengthens claim to title of greatest ever

**PARIS —** Roger Federer fell to his knees on the clay of Court Philippe Chatrier, overwhelmed by the achievement that had eluded him throughout his glittering career.

With a 6-1, 7-6 (1), 6-4 victory over Sweden’s Robin Soderling in the 2009 French Open final, Federer claimed his first championship at Roland Garros, completed the career Grand Slam and tied Pete Sampras’s record of 14 major men’s singles titles.

The result did more than fill the most conspicuous gap in Federer’s résumé. It substantially strengthened the argument that the Swiss star is the greatest male player in tennis history.

Federer became only the sixth man to win all four Grand Slam tournaments, joining Fred Perry, Don Budge, Rod Laver, Roy Emerson and Andre Agassi. More significantly, he achieved the feat in an era of increasingly specialized surfaces, deeper international competition and relentless physical demands.

“This might be my greatest victory, or certainly the one that takes the most pressure off my shoulders,” Federer said after receiving the trophy from Agassi, the last man before him to complete the career Grand Slam. “I think now, and until the end of my career, I can really play with my mind at peace.”

For years, Roland Garros had supplied the principal argument against Federer’s place at the top of the sport’s historical hierarchy. His dominance elsewhere was extraordinary: five consecutive Wimbledon titles, five consecutive U.S. Open championships and three Australian Open crowns. But the slow red clay in Paris repeatedly stopped him, most often in the form of Rafael Nadal.

Federer reached the French Open final in each of the previous three years and lost every time to Nadal, the Spaniard whose heavy topspin, speed and resilience made him nearly unbeatable on clay. Their 2008 final was particularly emphatic, with Nadal winning 6-1, 6-3, 6-0.

That history ensured that Federer arrived in Paris carrying more than the pressure of another major tournament. Each defeat revived questions about whether a player could be regarded as the greatest ever without winning the sport’s premier clay-court championship.

On Sunday, Federer removed that objection.

He did so with a composed and authoritative performance against Soderling, the player who had dramatically cleared Federer’s path by defeating Nadal in the fourth round. Nadal had never lost at Roland Garros before that match, winning the title in each of his first four appearances.

The absence of Nadal from the final will inevitably qualify some assessments of Federer’s triumph. Federer did not have to beat his greatest rival to win the trophy, and his losing record against Nadal — especially on clay — remained a significant part of any comparison between the two.

But championships are won by surviving the full tournament, not by defeating a preselected opponent. Federer still had to negotiate seven rounds, and his route was far from comfortable. He recovered from two sets to one down against Tommy Haas in the fourth round and from another deficit against Juan Martín del Potro in a five-set semifinal. At a tournament where expectation had become an annual burden, Federer held his nerve when his opportunity finally arrived.

Against Soderling, there was little sign of strain. Federer broke serve three times in the opening set and dominated the second-set tiebreak. His serve was especially effective, producing 16 aces and repeatedly preventing Soderling from establishing the powerful baseline rhythm that had unsettled Nadal.

Federer secured the championship with an ace on match point. Tears followed almost immediately.

The victory placed Federer level with Sampras at 14 major singles championships, then the leading total in men’s tennis history. Sampras accumulated his titles through commanding play at Wimbledon and the U.S. Open, but never won the French Open and reached the semifinals in Paris only once.

That contrast gives Federer a powerful advantage in the greatest-ever debate. He has now matched Sampras’s most celebrated numerical record while demonstrating success on every major surface. Federer has won on the hard courts of Melbourne and New York, the grass of Wimbledon and the clay of Paris.

Laver’s claim remains formidable. The Australian won the calendar-year Grand Slam twice, in 1962 and 1969, and lost some of his prime seasons at the majors because professionals were barred before the Open era. Bjorn Borg won six French Open titles and five consecutive Wimbledon championships, a remarkable combination of clay- and grass-court supremacy. Sampras spent a record 286 weeks as the world’s No. 1 and dominated much of the 1990s.

Comparisons across eras are inherently imprecise. Equipment, court speed, travel, training and tournament structures have all changed. No single victory can settle the argument.

Yet Federer’s case now combines historic totals with exceptional range and consistency. He has reached the final of every Grand Slam tournament multiple times and, by the end of this French Open, had appeared in a record 20 consecutive major semifinals. His blend of attacking skill, defense, movement and shot-making has allowed him to contend on every surface, even when the conditions did not naturally favor his most aggressive tennis.

The timing of the triumph also matters. Federer’s aura of invincibility had faded over the previous 18 months. Nadal had displaced him as the world’s leading player, beaten him in the 2008 Wimbledon final and again in the 2009 Australian Open final. Federer’s emotional reaction after the defeat in Melbourne raised questions about whether he could reverse the momentum of their rivalry.

In Paris, he answered a broader question. Even if Nadal had become the more difficult opponent and the stronger clay-court player, Federer was still capable of enduring pressure, adapting through difficult matches and seizing a historic opportunity.

At 27, Federer now stands one major title from surpassing Sampras. He will soon return to Wimbledon, where another championship would give him the men’s record outright.

But the importance of Sunday’s victory is not dependent on what comes next. Before this French Open, Federer’s record contained one obvious absence. After it, his résumé is complete: all four majors, 14 major titles and sustained excellence across the sport’s sharply different tests.

That does not end the debate over the greatest male player in history. It does, however, shift its terms. The burden is no longer on Federer to explain what he has not won. It is on the other candidates to show why their achievements outweigh the most comprehensive major-tournament record of the modern era.

**PARIS —** The scoreline was emphatic, but the argument it triggered will not be settled so easily.

Roger Federer defeated Robin Soderling 6-1, 7-6, 6-4 in the French Open final, completing the career Grand Slam and equalling Pete Sampras’s record of 14 major singles titles. In doing so, Federer filled the one conspicuous gap on his résumé and strengthened the case that he is the greatest men’s player in tennis history.

Sampras, whose benchmark Federer matched at Roland Garros, was in little doubt.

“What he’s done over the past five years has never, ever been done — and probably will never, ever happen again,” Sampras said. “Regardless if he won there or not, he goes down as the greatest ever. This just confirms it.”

The victory gave Federer his first French Open title after three consecutive final defeats to Rafael Nadal. This time Nadal was absent from the championship match, having lost to Soderling in the fourth round, but Federer still had to withstand the pressure of history and the expectations created by that upset.

He did so with a nearly flawless opening set, overwhelming Soderling in 23 minutes. The Swede offered more resistance in the second, yet Federer dominated the tie-break before securing an early break in the third and serving out the match.

Federer fell to his knees after match point, overcome by the significance of the moment. He had become only the sixth man to win all four major championships, joining Fred Perry, Don Budge, Rod Laver, Roy Emerson and Andre Agassi.

“It was probably my greatest victory,” Federer said. “It takes away so much pressure. I think now, and until the end of my career, I can really play with my mind at peace.”

Soderling, who had produced the tournament’s defining upset by ending Nadal’s unbeaten run at Roland Garros, was equally direct in his assessment of the champion.

“For me, he’s the best player in history,” Soderling said.

That view is supported by the breadth of Federer’s achievements. He has won on every surface, reached a record sequence of Grand Slam semifinals and appeared in 20 major finals. His style — built on balance, anticipation and a seemingly effortless range of shots — has also made him the standard by which modern all-court tennis is judged.

But “greatest ever” debates rarely turn on numbers alone. Sampras finished six consecutive seasons as world No. 1 and won 14 majors in an era of faster courts and sharply contrasting styles. Bjorn Borg collected 11 majors before retiring at 26. Rod Laver completed the calendar Grand Slam twice, though part of his prime fell during the years when professionals were barred from the major tournaments.

And then there is Nadal. The Spaniard held a winning record over Federer and had beaten him in major finals on clay, grass and hard courts. His five-set victory at Wimbledon in 2008 and his triumph over Federer at the 2009 Australian Open ensured that any claim of Federer’s supremacy would remain open to challenge.

Yet Roland Garros removed the strongest argument against him. Federer was no longer merely the dominant grass- and hard-court player of his generation. He was a champion at every major and the joint holder of the most important record in the men’s game.

Andre Agassi, the previous man to complete the career Grand Slam, praised both Federer’s achievement and the sustained excellence behind it.

“His accomplishments say it all,” Agassi said.

Federer can make the statistical argument even stronger by winning a 15th major. But after his victory over Soderling, the debate has shifted. The question is no longer whether Federer belongs beside Sampras, Laver and Borg.

It is whether any of them still belongs ahead of him.
